551.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
551.explanation: The monk Gardabhāli answers King Sañjaya, who has been hunting terrified deer in the royal park, by asking him to give other beings the same safety he wants for himself.
551.tie_back: The Kural calls a ruler who torments his subjects crueler than a murderer, and the Jain sage likewise confronts a king directly with his cruelty toward helpless beings.
551.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
551._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The rebuke of royal cruelty is direct, but its victims are animals in a hunt, not oppressed subjects.

552.quote_or_event: “A man who returns, as it were, to the vomit, is not praised; but you want to confiscate the property left by the Brâhmana.”
552.explanation: Queen Kamalāvatī shames King Ishukāra for trying to seize the property a Brahmin gave up when he renounced the world. Jacobi notes that confiscating heirless property was then a royal privilege.
552.tie_back: The Kural likens a king who demands his subjects' wealth to a highwayman with a spear. The queen likewise condemns a ruler's grab for his subjects' goods as shameful.
552.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
552._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi's text reads ‘returns, as it were,. to the vomit’ with a stray period, normalised here. The condemnation of royal seizure fits, but the robber image is the Kural's own.

553.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.”
553.explanation: The two Brahmin youths tell their father that every day lived without dharma is lost for good, so dharma cannot be put off.
553.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who fails to do justice every day sees his country decline every day, and the Jain verse makes the same day-by-day reckoning of what is lost when dharma is neglected.
553.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 14.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
553._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The emphasis on daily loss is close, but the verse concerns an individual's spiritual life, not a ruler's daily duty of justice.

554.quote_or_event: “In vain he adopts nakedness, who errs about matters of paramount interest; neither this world nor the next will be his; he is a loser in both respects in the world.”
554.explanation: The sage tells King Śreṇika that someone who errs about the things that matter most loses on both sides at once, in this life and the next.
554.tie_back: The Kural's thoughtless, unjust king loses his wealth and his people together, and the Jain verse likewise describes a wrong-doer who loses both things at once.
554.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 20.49 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
554._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Only the double-loss structure matches; the verse is about a false ascetic, not a ruler, so this is a next-best match.

555.quote_or_event: “Suffering, sorrow, agony, moaning, injury and lamentation, in oneself, in others or in both, lead to the influx of karmas which cause unpleasant feeling.”
555.explanation: Jain karma theory holds that causing others to grieve, weep and lament draws in karmic matter that later ripens as suffering for the one who caused it.
555.tie_back: The Kural says the tears of oppressed subjects are the weapon that wears away a tyrant's wealth. Jain doctrine also turns the victims' weeping back on the oppressor, through karma.
555.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.11, English rendering on jainworld.com (Tattvarth Sutra, Chapter 6)
555._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against jainworld.com; the page's typo ‘cuase’ is silently corrected to ‘cause’. The mechanism is impersonal karma rather than the immediate loss of wealth, but the link between causing tears and suffering retribution is close.

556.quote_or_event: “Sânti, a universal monarch of great power, the bringer of peace to the world, gave up Bharatavarsha and reached perfection.”
556.explanation: Gardabhāli's sermon lists righteous universal monarchs, such as Bharata, Sagara and Śānti, who are remembered for their virtue and for renouncing their power.
556.tie_back: The Kural says only just rule makes a king's fame endure, and the Jain list keeps the names of kings who brought peace to the world, though it values their renunciation more than their reigns.
556.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.38 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
556._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Enduring royal renown is only implied, and the verse praises giving up kingship rather than ruling justly, so this is a next-best match.

557.quote_or_event: “The customs, taxes, and confiscations were released, buying and selling prohibited, no policemen were allowed to enter houses, great and small fines were remitted, and debts cancelled.”
557.explanation: At Mahāvīra's birth King Siddhārtha also freed all prisoners, and the Kalpa Sūtra says the whole population of town and country rejoiced at this display of royal grace.
557.tie_back: The Kural says a king's lack of kindness is like drought to his people. Siddhārtha's festival shows the reverse: a king's kindness falling on his subjects like relief.
557.source: Kalpa Sūtra, Life of Mahāvīra §102 (with §100) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
557._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; a stray page-break character ‘I’ before ‘buying’ in the online text is omitted. This illustrates the Kural's point by showing its opposite, and the clemency is a festival measure, not a standing policy, so the match is partial.

558.quote_or_event: Kumārapāla, the Caulukya king of Gujarat who became a disciple of the Jain teacher Hemacandra, is remembered for abolishing the royal right to seize the property of people who died without heirs, which had left widows and families destitute.
558.explanation: Jain tradition presents the end of this confiscation as an act of compassion inspired by Jain teaching: the king stopped preying on his subjects' property.
558.tie_back: The Kural says that under an unjust king owning wealth is worse than poverty, because the owners are the ones who get stripped. Kumārapāla's reform removed one such predatory practice.
558.source: Kumarapala (Chaulukya dynasty), Wikipedia (summarising Jain prabandha sources)
558._accuracy_note: Wikipedia used as a last resort, only for this paraphrase. The underlying Jain prabandha texts were not checked this session. The reform answers the Kural's complaint directly but is a later historical tradition, not scripture.

559.quote_or_event: In the Jain account of the first age, the wishing-trees that had fed humanity lost their power ‘through the fault of time’, and only after that did people begin to break the laws and need a king to punish them.
559.explanation: Jain cosmology puts the decline of nature's bounty in the turning of the cosmic time cycle (avasarpiṇī), not in a ruler's moral failings.
559.tie_back: The Kural claims that when a king bends justice the seasons fail and rain stops. Jainism instead attributes natural decline to time itself and makes kings a response to that decline, not its cause.
559.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 1, ch. 2, part 8 ‘Coronation as king’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
559._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from Johnson's translation read on wisdomlib.org this session. Jain doctrine contradicts the Kural's claim that a king's injustice causes rain to fail, so this entry is a contrast, not a parallel.

560.quote_or_event: “A dreadful dearth prevailing about this time forced the monks to emigrate as far as the seaside. During these unsettled times they neglected their regular studies, so that the sacred lore was on the point of falling into oblivion.”
560.explanation: Hemacandra tells how a great famine in Candragupta's time scattered the Jain monks so that the canon was nearly forgotten, until the Saṅgha met at Pāṭaliputra to gather the eleven Aṅgas again.
560.tie_back: The Kural warns that when the land is not protected, the learned forget their scriptures, and Jain history records exactly that: in a time of public distress the monks almost lost their sacred texts.
560.source: Hemacandra, Pariśiṣṭaparvan IX.55–76, as summarised by Hermann Jacobi; quoted in ‘The Jain Church After Mahavira’, jainworld.com
560._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the jainworld.com page (Jacobi's summary, not a verse translation). Famine, not a king's neglect, is the cause here, and the Kural's point about cows' milk has no Jain counterpart.
